title: Aristides Writes His Own Name
text:
In classical Athens citizens could vote once a year to send one prominent man into exile for ten years. Each voter scratched a name on a piece of broken pottery, an ostrakon. Around 482 BC the vote turned against Aristides, a statesman so famous for his honesty that he was called "the Just".

Plutarch tells what happened on the day of the vote. An illiterate farmer, who did not know Aristides by sight, handed him his potsherd and asked him to write the name Aristides on it. Surprised, Aristides asked whether Aristides had ever done him any harm. The man said no, he did not even know him, but he was tired of hearing him called the Just everywhere.

Aristides said nothing, wrote his own name on the shard, and gave it back.

He was ostracized. As he left the city, Plutarch says, he prayed that Athens would never face a crisis that would make the people remember him. Two years later, with the Persians invading, Athens recalled its exiles, and Aristides fought at Salamis and commanded the Athenians at Plataea.
lesson: Keep acting honestly even toward people who are working against you. Your integrity is yours to keep, whatever they do.
